title: Moonlight like frost
hookLine: Li Bai sees moonlight before his bed like frost, looks up at the moon, and thinks of home
tomorrow: Li Bai drinks alone. who does he invite to make three?

cards: The first night in a new place is loud in a strange way: a fridge you don't know, a streetlight in the wrong window. The poet Li Bai, far from home, sees a pale patch on the floor before his bed. Frost?
No. Moonlight. He lifts his head and looks at the bright moon.
He lowers his head and thinks of home.

teach.b: That's the whole poem: four short lines, often called Quiet Night Thought. Watch the two movements. Head up, to the moon.
Head down, to home. The moon is the bridge, because it's the one thing hanging over his home as well. Why does home pull so hard?
In the Chinese tradition, home isn't only a place you came from. It's people you owe.

Confucius taught filial piety, xiao, the honor children owe their parents, and in the Analects he says, in Legge's English: "While his parents are alive, the son may not go abroad to a distance. If he does go abroad, he must have a fixed place to which he goes."
Leave if you must, but stay findable.
And the tradition's great festivals are homecomings: the reunion dinner at the New Year, and the Mid-Autumn night when families sit under the full moon together.
And when someone can't make it back, the same moon is how they keep the bond. Read that way, Li Bai's poem isn't weakness.
Thinking of home, in this tradition, is a kind of faithfulness: you lift your head, you lower it, and you're still someone's child.

how: In Chinese families, the New Year reunion dinner and the Mid-Autumn Festival under the full moon gather people home; Li Bai's Quiet Night Thought is learned by heart and said by people far from home.

o: a cold silver light used in temple lanterns
pale moonlight on Li Bai's floor that he took for frost
a hard frost that stops travelers on the winter road

games.q: the moon and home: tap the pairs.
p: the honor children owe their parents

s: Li Bai's poem is about a frosty winter night
it only looks like frost. it's moonlight on the floor.
Confucius says a child who travels should keep a fixed place to be found
the Analects: if he goes abroad, he must have a fixed place to which he goes.
in the poem, homesickness is a weakness to get over
head up to the moon, head down to home: the longing is part of loving your people.

games.q: your cousin is studying abroad and feels guilty for missing home on a festival night. what fits Li Bai?
o: look at the moon tonight; your family's under the same one.
missing home means you chose wrong; book a flight back.
don't think about home; it only makes the night worse.
games.why: in the Chinese tradition the shared moon keeps the bond when someone can't come home. thinking of home is faithfulness.

practice: Make Li Bai's two movements. Lift your head and look up: the sky, a window, the ceiling if that's what you've got. Then lower your head and think of home, whatever home means to you, a kitchen, a person, a street.
Stay there, head bowed, while you sit.

wordCard.voice: Moonlight like frost: the pale floor in Li Bai's poem, and the moon that hangs over home too.

orig.s: 床前明月光 疑是地上霜

orig.note: Chinese: before my bed, bright moonlight; I took it for frost on the ground. the opening of Li Bai's Quiet Night Thought.

carryVoice: Your line: thinking of home. In this tradition it's a kind of faithfulness. Good night, or good morning.
